In Which the Universe Refuses to Behave

The murder had not happened yet. This was, in itself, not especially alarming. Most murders, after all, have the elementary courtesy to occur before the paperwork arrives. The universe had declined to observe this courtesy. It rarely observed any, and never with an apology. In this respect it resembled most government departments, and several of Derek’s relatives. The resemblance was not considered flattering by any of the parties involved, though only the relatives had complained. The universe, as usual, had not been available for comment. Its press office had been closed for approximately thirteen point eight billion years, and the answering machine was full. Most murders have the decency to wait until after they happen before becoming administrative problems. The universe had, characteristically, declined to observe this convention. The universe, as usual, had not been consulted. The difficulty was that the Relativistic Investigation Bureau had already received the paperwork.
The time of death had been entered. The location had been entered. The victim had been identified.
The victim was Derek Gent. Derek was alive. He was also the sort of man who noticed discrepancies in official paperwork.
This particular discrepancy was rather difficult to ignore. The paperwork predicted his death three days before it was due to occur. Derek therefore did what any sensible investigator would do.
He checked the date, then the time, then the old clock.
Then the clock again, because the first check had produced a result he found professionally inconvenient. 11:17. The mysterious clock had stopped.

It had stopped at precisely the time printed on the murder notice. This would have been an excellent reason to panic if Derek had not already spent several years working in physics. Physicists are trained to distrust coincidences, measurements, clocks, diagrams, intuition and, when necessary, each other. This training has proved useful more often than is generally admitted, and has ruined more dinner parties than it has saved.

They are particularly suspicious of anything described as obvious. This suspicion has served the profession rather well. It has also made dinner parties more difficult than strictly necessary. Newton discovered that falling objects obeyed laws.

Einstein discovered that space and time did not behave the way Newton had imagined. General Relativity then made the still more inconvenient suggestion that gravity is deeply connected to the geometry of spacetime itself. None of this would have been especially troublesome if the universe had confined its eccentricities to respectable laboratories.
It did not. Clocks could disagree about elapsed time without either old clock being broken. Distances could depend on the observer.

Two observers could disagree about whether separated events were simultaneous. The speed of light could remain the same for all inertial observers. Gravity could alter the rate at which clocks accumulated proper time.

Curvature could reveal itself through the behaviour of neighbouring free-fall paths. And somewhere along the way, an ordinary cucumber became relevant. Nobody had intended this. In the Bureau’s experience, the most durable problems almost never began with anyone intending them. Intention, it turned out, was optional.

The universe had simply been uncooperative. It had a long and well-documented history of this. That was how the Relativistic Investigation Bureau came into existence. It was not founded because anyone had dreamed of becoming a civil servant.

Nobody dreams of becoming a civil servant. This is one of the few points on which the entire human species is in complete and suspicious agreement. The universe, for once, appears to share the sentiment — though it has never confirmed this in writing. Bureaus involve stationery, regulations, meetings, filing systems and the possibility that a perfectly respectable physical anomaly may be rejected because Form 17B had been completed in black ink instead of blue. The Relativistic Investigation Bureau existed because Derek Gent had begun asking questions.

Unfortunately, Derek was very good at asking them. There was Trevor Boltzman, who understood difficult mathematics but occasionally required a small verbal shove toward the obvious. There was Penny Gent, who could make tensor calculus sound almost reasonable and who regarded most forms of nonsense as a personal challenge.

There was Julius Barbarian, who maintained that time did not exist and had developed an argument for this that was considerably more coherent than anyone wanted it to be. There was Hermann Minkowski, who regarded spacetime as an entirely adequate explanation of itself and had no patience with people who demanded that it behave more intuitively. And there was Alfred Weinstein, who had somehow acquired the inconvenient habit of being the real inventor of Special and General Relativity in a universe where history insisted on crediting Einstein.
Weinstein regarded this as plagiarism on a cosmological scale. He had attempted to correct the historical record through ordinary academic channels. The academic channels had requested Form 17B.

Weinstein had never fully recovered. Then there was Sherlock. Sherlock was a dolphin. This was considered, within the Bureau, only moderately unusual — a fact that said rather more about the Bureau than about the dolphin. He was paid in fish, at the official rate of 1.7 fish per hour. He was hoping for 1.8. The relevant form had been pending since before the Pre-Transition drawer was
labelled. Most of the Bureau treated him as a remote consultant who occasionally sent useful geometry and then went back to thinking about fish.

Sherlock was also, according to Penny, the least improbable member of the Bureau once one had properly understood General Relativity. Nobody asked him to explain this. The Bureau had learned that explanations often made matters worse.

So when Derek found a murder notice announcing his own future death, he did not immediately conclude that he was being hunted by a time traveller, a quantum ghost or an unusually vindictive railway timetable. He began with the evidence. A stopped clock.
A future date. A murder that had not happened. And, eventually, a distant, mysterious train.

There was only one sensible response. Investigate. Because if the universe has made a mistake, someone has to fill in the form. The universe itself has never shown the slightest inclination to do so. It appears to regard paperwork as a purely human weakness, and possibly a form of performance art.
Preferably before 11:17. The universe, in Derek’s experience, rarely granted extensions, and never with an apology.
The Murder That Hadn’t Happened Yet

At precisely 9:17 on a Tuesday morning, Derek Gent received an email informing him that he was dead. He was not particularly surprised. Derek had always suspected that death would arrive by email. In this, as in so many other matters, he had been only slightly ahead of the general population — a position he found both comforting and faintly depressing, which was, on balance, better than the alternatives. The alternatives were rarely an improvement, a fact Derek had verified more than once, usually at personal cost and never with a sense of novelty.

Not because he was especially pessimistic, but because nearly everything important seemed to arrive by email these days. Electricity bills. Insurance renewals. Invitations to webinars. Notifications that someone had changed a password Derek had never used. Death was simply the logical next step. What surprised him was the sender.

The message had come from the Derek Gent Relativistic Investigation Bureau. Derek stared at the screen. The Bureau was not supposed to send him emails. Derek had written the rule himself, which made its violation particularly irritating.

It was his Bureau. More precisely, it was a small private investigative organization occupying two rooms on the second floor of an old office building in London, plus a corridor which the landlord insisted was a communal area and Derek insisted belonged to his Bureau whenever he needed somewhere to put a coat. The Bureau dealt primarily with unusual cases.
This was partly because Derek liked unusual cases and partly because ordinary cases paid terribly. The sign on the frosted glass door read:
And underneath that, added by Penny several years earlier:
NO MURDERS BEFORE 10 A. M. WITHOUT AN APPOINTMENT
Derek had objected. Penny had pointed out that they had never actually received a murder before ten.
Derek had said that this was beside the point.
Penny had stated that was precisely the point.
Derek had lost. He was now looking at an email from the Bureau. The subject line was:
We regret to inform you that you have been murdered.
The incident will occur tomorrow at 11:03 a. m. The perpetrator has been identified. It is you.
Then a third time. He glanced at the sender’s address. It was correct.
Then he stared at the Bureau’s computer. It was his computer.

Everything appeared to be where it ought to be, which was, in Derek’s experience, rarely a reliable indicator that everything was. The universe had a talent for looking organised just before it wasn’t. The filing cabinet was locked. The kettle was where the kettle normally was, which was not necessarily where it ought to be.
The window was shut, the door was shut, and nothing appeared to have been disturbed.

Derek gazed at the email again, with the particular stillness of a man who has just been handed a problem that refuses to sit neatly in any of the usual categories. The Bureau had categories for almost everything. This was not among them. A new category would no doubt be invented once the damage was complete. The Bureau was excellent at classifying disasters after the fact. Prevention had always been considered a secondary specialism, and occasionally an optional one. The official motto, never written down, was: “We’ll know what it was once it’s over.” No one had ever successfully ordered the motto in reverse.

Derek had once tried to summarise the Bureau’s actual remit on a single sheet of paper. The sheet had required three revisions, two appendices, and a footnote that began “In cases where the crime has not yet occurred…” He had eventually settled on a working definition: the Relativistic Investigation Bureau noticed things that ordinary agencies were structurally incapable of noticing, and then attempted to file them before they noticed back.

As for the purpose of everything, the Bureau’s unofficial position was that it was probably 42. No one had successfully derived the corresponding question, and the forms required to request it had been missing since before the Pre-Transition drawer was labelled.

There were, of course, children. The Bureau’s official position was that they were a long-term staffing solution and should be discouraged from developing an interest in geometry until after their GCSEs. Social security, like spacetime, required a continuous supply of new observers.
London supplied them without comment. The city had always been better at producing new observers than at agreeing what they were observing.
“That’s inconvenient,” he commented, as if the matter were primarily a filing error.

Across the empty room, Trevor Boltzman looked up. Trevor was twenty-eight, highly intelligent, technically qualified, and possessed of the unfortunate tendency to think about one problem at a time — a trait that made him excellent at mathematics and intermittently disastrous at life. He had a sister, Tabitha, who was generally considered the more dangerous of the two, a fact Trevor mentioned only when cornered, and sometimes not even then. Derek had met her once at a Bureau Christmas function that had refused to end on time. She had asked one question about simultaneous events and then left before anyone could answer it properly.
It made him considerably less useful when confronted with a sentence such as: “I have been murdered.”

Trevor removed his glasses — a gesture that, in the Bureau, usually preceded either insight or complete bafflement, with no reliable way of telling which in advance. Derek had stopped trying to predict it years ago. “What?”
“You’re telling me you’ve been murdered tomorrow?”
Derek waited. Trevor put his glasses back on. Derek continued waiting.
“I wasn’t sure what else to say. ‘Ah’ seemed to cover the available options.”
“How about ‘that’s impossible’? It has a certain traditional appeal.”
“I thought you’d already know that. You usually do.”
“Trevor, I have been working in this field for twenty-three years.”
“I know the difference between something being impossible and something being highly inconvenient.”
Trevor nodded and walked toward the kitchen. Derek called after him.
Trevor continued. Derek watched him disappear. A moment later there was a knock at the door.

Before Derek could answer, the door opened. Penny Gent, Derek’s cousin, stepped in without waiting for an invitation. She had never been much given to waiting for invitations, a trait that had served her well and other people less so. She also had the disconcerting ability to look as if she had somewhere more interesting to be, even when she was standing in a room full of stopped clocks. Derek had long since stopped minding. Resistance had proved inefficient. He had tried it once and found the paperwork excessive even by Bureau standards, which was saying something.

She was also one of those people who always appeared to have been designed specifically to make other people lose their train of thought. She was a striking brunette, though Derek had never used the word in her presence because he valued his life and had no particular desire to become the subject of a police report — or worse, a footnote. She wore a dark coat, carried a handbag, and had the calm expression of someone who had already dealt with several irritating people before breakfast and was prepared, if necessary, to deal with several more.
“Like you’ve just discovered the Inland Revenue has found you.”
She walked over to the computer.
Derek turned the monitor toward her. Penny read the email. Her expression changed.
Only slightly. Penny was clever. Very clever.

Unlike Trevor, who approached every new piece of information as if it might require a spreadsheet, Penny seemed to absorb things almost before anyone had spoken. She read the mysterious message again.
“I’d hate to think you’d become predictable.”
He smiled lightly, somewhat against his own will. Trevor came back carrying three mugs.
Then he handed Derek the other one. Derek took a sip before looking sharply at Trevor.
“I thought there were only two of us.”
Penny met his gaze. Trevor regarded Penny. Then at Derek.
“She’s been here for approximately ninety seconds.”
“And yet somehow you’ve already forgotten that she exists,” countered Derek.
Trevor stared silently at Derek’s mug.
Penny smiled, clearly amused. “Don’t worry. He’s usually this bright.”

Derek turned back to the computer. Something was still bothering him, and it was not the murder itself. Murders, at least, had the virtue of being conclusive. This felt more like an administrative error with fatal consequences — the sort of thing the Bureau specialised in, usually without the fatal part. The fatal part was considered an over-performance. The Bureau preferred its disasters to remain administrative — they were easier to file, and considerably harder to explain at the inquest. The Bureau disliked inquests almost as much as it disliked surprises. Both had a tendency to generate unanswered questions, and unanswered questions had a tendency to generate more forms. The Bureau considered this a feature. Features, in the Bureau’s vocabulary, were problems that had learned to fill in their own forms. Some of them had started applying for promotion. One had reportedly made it onto a shortlist before anyone noticed it did not exist. The panel had scored it highly for clarity of objectives.
The murder was, in some respects, straightforward. The date was the problem. He clicked the attachment.

A photograph appeared. For a moment Derek stopped breathing. The room felt briefly smaller, as if the air itself had taken an interest. He recognised the feeling: it was the same one that arrived just before a theory collapsed, or a relationship, or both. Somewhere beneath the professional irritation, something colder and more personal had stirred — the quiet recognition that the face in the photograph was not merely a case, but a deadline. Derek had never liked deadlines that looked back at him. Most deadlines had the decency to remain abstract. The photograph itself felt like a decohered outcome: one possibility selected, the others no longer available for inspection. It had the quiet finality of a decision the universe had made without consulting the minutes. Derek filed the sensation under ‘to be examined later’ and continued working. He was good at filing things under ‘later’. It was one of his more reliable skills, and possibly one of his more dangerous ones. Trevor noticed.
Derek turned the monitor toward them. The photograph showed their office. Not a similar office.
Not a room that resembled it. The actual room. The same battered desk.
The same green filing cabinet. The same window overlooking the street. The same framed photograph of Derek’s grandfather standing beside a Morris Minor in 1964.
And on the floor, face-down beside the familiar desk, was Derek. There was blood on the back of his shirt. Trevor stared intently.
“Because it would be a very poor photograph if I didn’t.”
Trevor zoomed in. “There’s something on the desk.”

Derek peered at the screen. A small, silent brass railway clock stood beside the computer, looking entirely ordinary and entirely wrong, which was, in Derek’s experience, the most dangerous combination. He had the sudden, unwelcome sense that the clock had been waiting for him.
Derek looked again. The old clock showed 11:03. He inspected the clock on his own desk. 9:21.
His phone and the wall clock both read 9:21.
He looked back at the photograph. 11:03.
Trevor frowned. “Then when was it taken?”
Derek pointed at the picture. “The clock reads eleven-oh-three.”
“And the photograph was apparently taken at the moment of my death.”
Trevor waited. Derek glanced at him. Trevor turned back.
“Trevor, you really must learn to recognise a mystery when it is standing on the table waving its arms.”
“If it’s a photograph taken tomorrow, then why does the clock show eleven-oh-three?”
“So, the photograph was taken two hours later.”
Trevor wore the pleased expression of a man who had just solved something. “That’s what I meant.”

Trevor’s expression collapsed with the quiet dignity of a man who has just watched a carefully constructed theory meet reality and lose. It was a look Derek had come to recognise, and almost respect. “Oh.”
Derek got up and walked to the window. Outside, gloomy London was doing what London did best: being grey, getting wet, and charging for the privilege.
Also, being expensive and mildly annoying.
A bus stopped, and another stopped behind it; neither seemed to know why. Derek watched the traffic. London was, as usual, being mildly inconvenient.
Penny raised her eyes. “Your impending murder?”
Penny gazed at him. Trevor immediately reconsidered his life choices.
He pointed toward the street. “Everyone assumes time is the same everywhere.”
“Because Alfred Weinstein ruined that particular assumption.”
Penny sat down. “Would you care to explain?”
Derek picked up a marker and went to the whiteboard.

“This is basic Special Relativity — the part that still manages to surprise people who thought they already understood time. They almost never have, you see. Watch. Time turns out to be less a river than a set of carefully negotiated local agreements between observers who have never actually met… and would probably dislike each other if they did. The agreements are enforced by the speed of light, which accepts no appeals and keeps no office hours. It is the only absolute the Bureau has never successfully filed a complaint against.”
“That last part isn’t in the textbooks.”
He looked at the board again.
“That’s usually how the dangerous ones start. The safe ones come with references.”
Trevor wrote the sentence down anyway, under Provisional.
He drew a railway track. Then a mysterious train. “Suppose you’re standing on a platform and a train passes you at a very high speed.”
He drew two lightning bolts. “Lightning strikes the front and rear of the train simultaneously.”
“An observer standing on the platform, exactly halfway between the two strikes, sees the flashes arrive simultaneously.”
“Now imagine someone sitting exactly halfway between the front and rear of the train.”
“So, the passenger is moving toward the flash at the front and away from the flash at the back.”
Trevor nodded. “The front flash reaches him first.”
Trevor frowned sharply. “But the lightning still struck at the same time.”
Derek smiled. “According to whom?” he asked Trevor.

“Different observers can disagree about whether two separated events happened at the same time. Neither is wrong. The universe simply refuses to appoint a referee. It’s never shown any interest in the job. Applications are not being accepted. They never have been. The position remains permanently vacant. Candidates are discouraged from applying. The discouragement is considered permanent. The universe simply declines to supply a single, universal ‘now’ — a fact that continues to inconvenience anyone who prefers their reality tidy. Most people prefer it tidy. The universe has never taken this preference into account, and shows no sign of starting. It has, however, been very consistent about this — consistency being one of its few reliable vices. Unreliability would have been more interesting, but less characteristic. The universe preferred to be boring in ways that were fatal.”
Trevor studied the photograph. “You’re saying there’s no universal ‘now’.”
Derek put the marker down. “Not in Special Relativity. And that matters here more than most people are prepared to notice.”
Penny looked again at the vivid photograph. “Because the murder is an event.”
“And the timestamp is an observation of that event.”
“So, we need to know the reference frame.”
Derek nodded. “Now you’re thinking like a detective.”
Trevor raised a finger. “Wouldn’t the photograph itself give us the frame?”

“Light takes time to reach the camera. That’s obvious — until you realise how many conclusions quietly depend on pretending it doesn’t. The camera, like every other observer, is trapped inside its own light-cone and has never been consulted about the matter. Cameras are surprisingly philosophical once you notice this. Most of them just keep it to themselves.”
Trevor stopped. Derek could see the thought arriving. “Ah.”
“So, even the photograph isn’t necessarily showing us what happened when we think it happened. The camera, like every other observer, is trapped inside its own light-cone.”
“Correct.” Derek sat down. “And that’s where things become interesting.”
He enlarged the photograph. There was something in the lower-right corner. A piece of paper.
He zoomed in. It contained three lines.
Derek zoomed in again. The railway silent clock in the photograph wasn’t showing exactly 11:03. It showed 11:03:17.
Derek stared intently. He looked at his own clock. 9:27:17.
He checked his phone. 9:27:17. The wall clock.
“Seventeen seconds.” He said it quietly, as if the number itself might change if spoken too loudly. In the Bureau, numbers that behaved themselves were considered mildly suspicious.
“Because if this were simply a badly set clock, there’s no reason for the seconds to line up.”
Penny fixed him with a look. Trevor immediately reconsidered his life choices.
Derek opened the Bureau’s internal records. The system showed no record of the ancient brass clock. No purchase.
No inventory entry. No photograph. No mention of it.
Derek searched the building’s security footage. Nothing. He checked the office camera.
At 9:16, the old desk was empty. At 9:17, the old desk was empty. At 9:18, the desk was empty.
At 9:19, the old desk was empty. At 9:20, the ancient brass clock appeared. Trevor stared.
Derek replayed it. The clock simply suddenly appeared. There was no hand.
There was no person and no shadow. One frame showed nothing.
The next showed the clock. Penny watched Derek.
Penny studied it again, more carefully this time. It did. The shadow moved normally as the light from the window changed.
Derek replayed the footage. The silent clock existed. Then it didn’t.
Then it existed again. Trevor’s expression deteriorated by degrees.
“So, how do we know anything is real?”
Derek met his eyes. “Now you’re asking the right question.”
Trevor didn’t look reassured. Derek slowly opened another file.
He took the ancient brass clock from the photograph and compared its mechanism with the Bureau’s clocks. They were different. He compared the hands.
Different. He compared the second hand. Identical.
Seventeen seconds. Derek frowned. Penny noticed.
Derek turned the clear photograph upside down. There was a small number written on the back. 1047.
He reviewed the case database. Case 1047 did not exist. He searched deleted cases.
Nothing. He searched archived cases. Nothing.
He searched future-dated cases. Nothing. Then the computer made a noise.
A soft chime. A new case appeared.
Derek stared intently. Penny leaned over.
Derek scrolled. The case contained only three pieces of information. Client: Derek Gent.
There was one note. Written in Derek’s own handwriting.
DO NOT LET TREVOR NEAR THE STRANGE CLOCK.
Penny smiled. “This is becoming quite good.”
“Someone—or something—is creating cases inside our system.”
Derek turned the monitor toward them. The address read:
“So, someone is doing it from here.”
Penny surveyed the room. There were three people in it. Derek.
Derek looked at the three chairs. Then the silent clock. Then the computer.
“Or one of us hasn’t done it yet.”

Derek regarded her. The office suddenly felt colder. Not the ordinary London cold — something more precise, as if a draft had found its way in from a place that did not appear on any map. Trevor swallowed.
Derek didn’t answer. The computer chimed again. All three studied the screen.
Derek opened it. The name appeared.
Derek gave him a measured look. Trevor and Penny exchanged a glance.
Derek glanced at the clock. 9:31:17. He stared at the photograph.
11:03:17. He returned to the case file. Then he looked at Trevor.
Derek walked to the whiteboard. He wrote:
“Before we worry about who did it, we need to know what actually happened.”
Penny regarded him carefully. “Do you understand?”
Trevor thought for a while. “I think so.”
Derek picked up his coat. The decision, once made, felt both inevitable and slightly unreal.
“Then we’re going to need to leave.”
“So, whoever put it here expected us to find it.”
Trevor stood. “All right, then, where are we going?”
Derek held up the photograph. “To the place where it came from.”
Penny grabbed her coat. “And where is that?”
Derek turned the photograph over. On the back, beneath the number 1047, another line had suddenly appeared.
Trevor surveyed the photograph. “And that’s after you’re dead.”
“So, how are we supposed to investigate it?”
Derek smiled. “We’ll have to be there.”
Trevor thought for a moment. “How do we know we’ll get there?”
Derek opened the door. “Because someone has already told us that we will.”
Penny followed him. Trevor remained where he was.
“Then we’ll have wasted a perfectly good morning.”
“Then I suppose I’ll have to solve my own murder. The words sounded almost reasonable until one considered them.”

They stepped into the corridor. Mrs Marsh, the building superintendent, was already there, polishing a non-existent mark on the wall with the air of someone who had been waiting specifically to be inconvenient. She was widely regarded as the most immovable object in the building, and possibly in several adjacent dimensions. She did not look up. “You’re tracking geometry in again,” she said.

Further down the corridor, Mr Pendleton from Facilities stood with a clipboard and the expression of a man who had already decided the answer was no. He specialised in a different kind of obstruction: the kind that required signatures, countersignatures, and the quiet insistence that whatever you needed was in a different section, a different building, or a different continuum. The heavy door closed behind them with the finality of a decision that had already been made somewhere else. Inside the empty office, the old brass clock appeared on Derek’s desk as if it had been waiting for the room to be unoccupied.
Its second hand moved. One. Two.
Then continued. But now the clock was showing 11:03. And outside the empty office, somewhere far away, a distant train whistle sounded.
There was no railway empty station anywhere near the building. The whistle sounded again. Then a third time.
The Bureau’s computer switched itself on. A final message appeared.
And beneath it, in smaller letters:
DO NOT LET WEINSTEIN GET TO THE EMPTY STATION FIRST.
The message disappeared. The screen went black. Then the computer displayed the date.
The quiet office was empty. For the moment.
By Wednesday morning, Derek Gent had decided that there were two kinds of impossible. The first kind was the ordinary sort. A man could not be in two places at once.

A clear photograph could not normally exist before it was taken. A clock could not run backwards without either being broken or being subjected to a level of engineering that Derek considered unnecessarily ambitious. The second kind was considerably worse.

The second kind was something that was perfectly consistent with the laws of physics but completely inconsistent with common sense. Derek had spent most of his professional life dealing with the second kind. He found it much more expensive.

At 8:36 on Wednesday morning, he was standing in front of the whiteboard in the Bureau while Trevor sat at the old desk and Penny leaned against the window. The brass railway clock sat between them. It had arrived sometime during the night.
Nobody had seen it arrive. Nobody knew where it had come from. And it was still showing 11:03:17.
Derek had written three words on the board.
“The first thing we need to establish,” he explained, “is what actually happened.”
“Not necessarily. You may be putting the cart before the flaming horse.”
“We have a photograph of you lying dead.”
“We have a second timestamp in the Bureau.”
“Because we don’t know whether they are supposed to agree.”
Penny smiled. Derek inspected Trevor. Trevor immediately raised both hands.
“You were not.” Trevor sighed. “I was merely testing the waters.” Derek found his eyes. “You were throwing the fish tank into the river.”
He labelled one A and the other B.
“These happen somewhere in spacetime. We can describe each event by four coordinates.”
He wrote: x, y, z, t Trevor nodded.
“And different observers can assign different coordinates.”
“Because they’re moving relative to one another.”
“So, the question isn’t simply when Derek died.”
“It’s when Derek died according to which observer.”
“I think so.” Penny smiled. “Good. You’ve hissed all my mystery lectures, and now one has finally landed.”
“But the death itself either happened or it didn’t.”
“That part doesn’t depend on the observer.”
“Because light has to travel from the event to the camera.”
“So, the photograph doesn’t show the event itself.”
“It shows light arriving from the event.”
“Which means the image contains information about an earlier event.”
“So, when we say the photograph was taken at 11:03, we’re already making an assumption about the relationship between the clock and the event.”
Penny laughed. Derek walked to the old desk and picked up the ancient brass clock. He turned it over.
There was a small metal plate on the back. No manufacturer’s name. No serial number.
Derek handed it to her. She examined it carefully.
“More precise than it has any right to be.”
She handed the silent clock back.
Trevor took it. He examined the back.
Derek took the clock from him. Trevor was right. The casing was too thin.
There was nowhere to put anything substantial. Derek turned it over again. The second hand moved.
Derek turned his attention to him.
“So, seventeen is part of the message.”
“Seventeen kilometres per second. Seventeen percent of something. Seventeen metres per second. There’s no shortage of seventeen in physics.”
Trevor realized he had announced something interesting.
“If seventeen seconds is a proper-time interval…”
“Then we’d need to know which worldline we’re talking about,” Penny asserted.
“Which means we’re already getting ahead of ourselves.”
“We need the simplest possible explanation first.”
“Do you ever find it strange saying that?”
“That you’re using Weinstein’s equations to investigate a case involving Weinstein’s own theory.”
“Because if you want to investigate a crime involving gravity, you use General Relativity.”
“If you want to investigate a crime involving relative motion and time, you use Special Relativity.”
“Then you start charging by the hour.”
Penny laughed. Derek pointed to the first equation.
“And the important bit is that t’ depends on x.”
“Meaning that time in one frame depends partly on where the event occurs in the other frame.”
“So, two events that are simultaneous in one frame need not be simultaneous in another.”
Penny pointed out, “Which is relativity of simultaneity.”
Derek glanced at the photograph again.
“And that is the first thing I want to test.”
He opened the Bureau’s sophisticated analysis software.
“Suppose the photograph corresponds to an actual event tomorrow at 11:03:17.”
“And suppose the camera and the Bureau are moving relative to one another.”
“Then the time coordinate assigned to that event could be different in the two frames.”
Trevor clarified, “But unless they’re moving at a substantial fraction of the speed of light, the difference should be tiny.”
“Small enough that London Underground timetables are generally a greater source of temporal uncertainty.”
“So, ordinary motion can’t explain a difference of nearly two hours.”
Derek entered the relevant numbers. The computer calculated. He studied the result.
Then he entered them again. Trevor watched.
“So, Special Relativity is telling us the premise is wrong.”
Trevor slowly gazed at the equation.
“Could the photograph be showing a different event?”

A Completely Respectable Explanation of What Has Just Happened

By now you have encountered clocks that disagree, trains that arrive before they leave, corridors that acquire extra doors, cold rain that occasionally develops opinions, cucumbers, holograms, singularities, dolphins, and a man who apparently exists in more than one place. And you’re probably wondering whether any of this has anything at all to do with real physics. Well… annoyingly, yes. Quite a lot of it does.

Now, the point of this appendix isn’t just to tell you what the characters were talking about. The point is that when you’re done, you should be able to explain the central ideas yourself. Each chapter therefore does four things. First, it states the idea in ordinary language.

Second, it gives you the physics underneath the joke. Third, it points out the most tempting way to misunderstand it. Fourth, it gives you a tiny test. If you can answer that test, you have learned something rather than merely survived it.
You do not need university-level mathematics to understand the central ideas. You need arithmetic. A little algebra.
And the ability to accept that the universe does not care what you personally think “obviously” means.

One useful rule will appear repeatedly: separate what an observer measures from what the theory requires is invariant. Another is even more important: when a metaphor helps you understand the physics, keep the metaphor. When the metaphor starts making predictions… throw it away. The cucumber, for example, is an excellent teacher.
It is not a peer-reviewed vegetable.
Before We Begin — The Twin Paradox

Here is the classic version. One twin boards a very fast spaceship, travels out and back near the speed of light, and returns to find their sibling considerably older. Both twins, the objection runs, saw the other one moving — so shouldn’t each of them expect the other to have aged less? Surely it cannot be true for both.

It cannot, and it isn’t. The two twins do not take the same route through spacetime between their parting and their reunion — only the travelling twin’s path bends, out and back, while the twin on the sofa travels a straight, unaccelerated line between the same two events. That is the entire resolution: proper time depends on the path taken, not merely on relative motion, and the straight path between two events always racks up more of it than any bent one. Turning around is what makes the paths different — it is not, by itself, what makes the travelling twin younger. There is a genuine fact about which twin aged less, and it belongs to whoever took the bent path.

This is the same idea as the invariant spacetime interval you are about to meet in Chapter 2, wearing a different coat. Proper time, like ordinary distance, depends on the path you actually take. Drive the direct road between two towns and you burn less petrol than the driver who takes the scenic route, even though both of you started and finished in the same two places. Nobody finds that paradoxical. The twin paradox is exactly this, except the odometer is a wristwatch and the scenic route is nearly the speed of light.

Which brings us, unavoidably, to the other Derek, first glimpsed in Chapter 11 and interrogated properly in Chapter 14. Whatever else was happening on that train, only one Derek could be right about how much time had passed since the two of them last shared a worldline. The Bureau has not yet worked out which one. Trevor has helpfully suggested filing the question under Pending Geometry, alongside the wormhole.
Chapter 1 — Special Relativity Begins by Being Rude
The first thing to understand about Special Relativity is that it does not begin with the statement:
That is a popular summary and is also rather misleading. Einstein’s Special Relativity rests on two principles: The laws of physics are the same in all inertial reference frames.
The speed of light in vacuum is the same for all inertial observers. It’s the second one that causes all the trouble. Suppose you are sitting on a distant train.
You throw a ball forward at 10 m/s. Someone standing on the platform sees the ball moving at roughly: train speed + 10 m/s.
Perfectly ordinary. Now replace the ball with light.
Classical intuition replied that the person on the platform should measure:
train speed + speed of light. Nature responds:
The light still travels at exactly (c). This forces us to abandon the old assumptions about space and time. And that is where things become interesting.

Here is the classic way to see why — not just that it is true, but why it comes out as an actual number. Imagine a clock built from a single photon of light, bouncing straight up and down between two mirrors a fixed distance apart. Each round trip is one ‘tick.’ Nothing exotic: light, two mirrors, geometry.

Now put that clock on the mysterious train, moving past a platform at speed v. From Trevor’s point of view, standing on the platform, the light doesn’t simply go straight up and down — the train is moving, so the photon has to travel diagonally to keep up with the departing mirror, tracing a longer zigzag path for each tick.

Here is the part that actually causes the trouble. The speed of light does not change for Trevor either. Longer path, same speed, more time. That is the whole derivation. One tick of the train’s clock, measured from the platform, simply takes longer than one tick measured on the train. Do the geometry properly — a right triangle, Pythagoras, nothing worse — and out drops exactly the same γ you are about to meet properly in the next chapter, without asking anyone to take the mathematics on faith.
This is why time dilation is not a story about clocks getting confused. It is what geometry does when one side of the triangle refuses to change length no matter how fast you are moving.

None of this is hypothetical. The satellites that make a phone’s map work are moving fast enough, and sitting high enough out of Earth’s gravity well, that both effects discussed in this book — Special Relativity’s time dilation from speed, and General Relativity’s time dilation from gravity — apply to their onboard clocks simultaneously, pulling in opposite directions. Engineers correct for it deliberately, every single day, or a phone’s position would drift by several kilometres within hours. The Bureau finds this less remarkable than most people do. The Bureau finds most things less remarkable than most people do.

Common trap: “Relative” does not mean “anything goes.” The spacetime interval and other invariant quantities remain the same. Quick test: If two inertial observers disagree about simultaneity, must one of their clocks be broken? No.

Special Relativity deals with inertial frames and flat spacetime. But gravity causes a problem. Einstein noticed something wonderfully simple:

If you are inside a freely falling lift, you cannot locally distinguish falling freely in a gravitational field from drifting weightlessly in empty space, far from any gravity. This is the equivalence principle. Imagine dropping a ball inside a falling lift.
The ball and the lift are both falling. So, relative to you, the ball simply floats. Now imagine the lift is far away from any gravitational field and accelerating upward.
You release the ball. It appears to fall toward the floor. Locally, the two situations can look identical.
That suggested something profound: Perhaps gravity isn’t fundamentally a conventional force. Perhaps it is geometry.
General Relativity makes precisely that leap. Matter and energy affect spacetime geometry. Objects then move through that geometry.
The famous slogan is: Matter tells spacetime how to curve; spacetime tells matter how to move. That is considerably more accurate than blaming gravity on the apple.
Although the apple remains available for consultation.

Keep this: General Relativity replaces flat spacetime with a dynamical geometry that responds to matter and energy. Common trap: The equivalence principle is local. A sufficiently small freely falling laboratory can mimic an inertial frame, but tidal effects reveal curvature over larger regions. Quick test: What tells you that a gravitational field cannot be removed everywhere just by choosing an accelerating frame? Tidal effects.
Chapter 4 — Time May Be Less Fundamental Than You’d Like

Julius Barbarian’s claim that time does not exist is deliberately provocative. But there is serious physics hiding underneath the joke. In relativity, there is no single universal time shared by the entire universe.
Different observers can experience different amounts of proper time between events. Proper time is the time measured by a clock travelling along a particular worldline. So, instead of asking:
“How much proper time elapsed along this particular path through spacetime?”
That is a much better question. And General Relativity goes further. Gravitational fields affect the rate at which clocks run relative to one another.

a strange clock deeper in a gravitational field can accumulate less proper time than one farther away. So, clocks do not merely measure some universal substance called Time. They measure something associated with their physical histories.
Barbarian therefore has a point. Unfortunately, he also has an alarming tendency to explain it while eating biscuits.
Keep this: Relativity removes universal Newtonian time; each clock measures proper time along its own worldline.
Common trap: Saying ‘time is not real’ goes beyond what relativity itself establishes.
Quick test: Can two clocks follow different paths through spacetime and accumulate different proper times? Yes.
The object is following a natural path through curved spacetime. That natural path is called a geodesic. On the surface of the Earth, an orbiting spacecraft is actually in free fall.
It is not being “held up” by a mysterious absence of gravity.

It is following its geodesic. The astronauts inside feel weightless because they are falling together with the spacecraft. The surface of the Earth prevents us from following our natural free-fall path.
The floor pushes upward on our feet. Which is why standing still is, in a relativistic sense, rather more strenuous than orbiting Earth.
The apple was therefore not really falling because gravity “pulled” it downward in the Newtonian sense.
It was following the geometry. Newton wasn’t wrong. He had simply discovered an extraordinarily good approximation to something deeper.

Keep this: Newtonian gravity is an extraordinarily successful approximation; General Relativity gives the deeper geometric description. Common trap: Do not say Newton was simply wrong. Newtonian gravity remains an excellent approximation when relativistic corrections are small.
Quick test: Why do astronauts in orbit feel weightless? They and their spacecraft are in free fall.
Here Derek makes an important distinction. A singularity is not simply a place where gravity is very strong. That would be too easy.

A singularity represents a breakdown of the classical spacetime description. One useful way of expressing this is through geodesic incompleteness. Imagine following a freely falling observer’s worldline.

Normally, you should be able to keep extending that path. At a singularity, the classical theory can tell you that the path simply cannot be continued in the expected way. That tells us something profound:
The theory has reached its limit. This is why physicists don’t normally say:
“There’s a really strong gravitational field over there, so that’s a singularity.”

They ask whether the mathematical structure of spacetime itself becomes pathological. And that distinction matters enormously when we discuss black holes and the early universe. A singularity is not necessarily an object sitting somewhere waiting to be photographed.
It may be telling us that General Relativity is incomplete at that point. Which is physicist-speak for:
“The equations have stopped being helpful. Someone should probably invent some better ones.”

Keep this: A singularity is best understood as a failure or incompleteness of the classical spacetime description. Black holes contain singularities (classically) hidden behind event horizons. White holes are the time-reverse: regions that can only emit, never absorb. Wormholes are hypothetical tunnels connecting distant regions of spacetime; the simplest versions are the Einstein-Rosen bridges that appear in the maximally extended black-hole geometry. Most wormholes in classical general relativity are non-traversable. Keeping one open long enough to walk through requires exotic matter that violates energy conditions.

In this story the Underground’s stranger geometry occasionally behaves as if it were flirting with all three: a breakdown of the classical description (singularity), a one-way refusal to let certain paths return (white-hole-like), and a shortcut that should not exist (wormhole-like). The Bureau’s official position is that the Underground is merely having a bad day.
Common trap: A singularity is not merely a region where gravity happens to be extremely strong.
Quick test: What should a singularity make you suspect? That the classical theory has reached its limit.
Chapter 7 — Why SR and GR Don’t Fight

General Relativity contains Special Relativity locally. In a sufficiently small region of spacetime, a freely falling observer can construct a local inertial frame. Within that small region, physics looks like Special Relativity.
So: SR = local flat-spacetime physics while
GR = the larger theory describing curved spacetime and how those local frames fit together. This is why the theories can coexist perfectly well.
The Underground was therefore not going to discover that SR was “wrong.”
It was more likely to reveal that Derek had chosen a sufficiently inconvenient coordinate system. This is an important distinction.
Keep this: Special Relativity is the local limit of General Relativity in freely falling frames.

Common trap: GR does not make SR obsolete. It contains local SR while describing how local frames fit together in curved spacetime. Quick test: Why can a small freely falling laboratory behave approximately like Special Relativity? Because curvature effects become negligible over a sufficiently small region.

It is also an excellent metaphor for something real. Physics is full of boundaries between descriptions. An observer may describe an object as being in one place while another observer assigns different coordinates to it.
The underlying physics doesn’t change merely because the description changes. This is another recurring lesson: A coordinate description is not an invariant physical fact.
If the Bureau’s doors behaved like spacetime coordinates, Derek could quite legitimately say:
“The door is open in my coordinate system.”
Trevor would then require the aforementioned slap.
Keep this: Coordinates are descriptions. Changing coordinates does not by itself change the physical situation.
Common trap: A metaphor about doors, maps or languages is not itself a coordinate transformation.
Quick test: If two coordinate systems assign different numbers to the same event, does that automatically mean two different events occurred? No.
Picture a spaceship travelling at relativistic speed. Its clock measures its own proper time. An observer on Earth measures a different elapsed time. The relationship involves the Lorentz factor:

This produces time dilation. It also produces length contraction in the direction of motion. But remember:
Nobody experiences their own clock as running slowly. Your own clock always appears normal to you. It is the comparison between different worldlines that produces the effect.

If Derek flies to another star at enormous speed and returns, he might have aged considerably less than people who stayed on Earth. This is not because his watch malfunctioned. His watch correctly measured his proper time.
And this is why booking Ryanair is not actually an established method of achieving relativistic time travel. The airline has, so far, declined to comment.

Common trap: Time dilation is not a malfunction of the travelling clock, and the traveller does not watch their own clock run abnormally slowly. The ordinary cucumber is useful because it is boring. Boring objects are excellent physics experiments. If you move an ordinary cucumber rapidly relative to an observer, Special Relativity predicts that its measured length along the direction of motion is contracted by a factor of 1/γ.
The ordinary cucumber itself does not feel squashed. Its own rest-frame measurement remains unchanged. Again:
Different observers assign different measurements. But the underlying relativistic structure is consistent. And this is precisely why the cucumber becomes such a useful running joke.
It is an ordinary object. If the ordinary cucumber obeys relativity, so does the universe. Probably.
The ordinary cucumber has, however, declined to comment. This is probably for the best.

Common trap: The moving cucumber does not discover itself physically squashed. Its rest-frame length remains L₀. Now we enter much more speculative territory. The holographic principle arose from thinking about black-hole entropy. Black holes have an entropy proportional to the area of their event horizon, not simply the volume inside.

That suggested something extraordinary: Perhaps the information describing a region of space can be encoded on its boundary. In certain theories, this idea becomes mathematically precise — but not as a general statement that our universe is literally a hologram.

The most famous example is AdS/CFT duality, associated especially with Juan Maldacena. Very roughly: A gravitational theory in a higher-dimensional spacetime can be equivalent to a quantum field theory without gravity living on a lower-dimensional boundary.

This does not mean the universe is literally a two-dimensional cinema screen. It means that two apparently different mathematical descriptions can encode the same underlying physics. And that connects beautifully with relativity.

In Special Relativity, different observers use different coordinates. In General Relativity, different coordinate systems can describe the same geometry. In holographic duality, dramatically different-looking theories can describe the same physical system.
The common philosophical lesson is: A description is not necessarily the same thing as the underlying physical system it describes.
Penny watching Everything Everywhere All at Once therefore doesn’t prove holography.

It merely gives her an unusually entertaining way of thinking about different descriptions of reality. And Jamie Lee Curtis proves nothing whatsoever. Except possibly that Hollywood has its own theory of conservation of actresses.
Keep this: The holographic principle is motivated by black-hole entropy, and in special settings such as AdS/CFT it becomes a precise duality.
Common trap: This does not establish that our universe is literally a two-dimensional cinema screen.
Quick test: What is the important lesson of a duality? Two very different mathematical descriptions can encode the same physical system.

So, she does the sensible thing about a man who is annoyingly correct. She goes to the cinema. Alone.

First, the disclaimer Penny makes herself: the film’s multiverse is not the multiverse that occasionally shows up in serious physics. None of them look remotely like a laundromat, and you do not need to know a single one of their names to follow this chapter.

The film is a storytelling device, not a scientific interpretation of quantum mechanics. Treat it exactly the way you would treat the ordinary cucumber: an excellent aid to intuition and completely inadmissible as evidence. What the film is quietly useful for is an idea this book has been building since Chapter 2. It doesn’t need a single equation. Physics is not tied to one particular coordinate description. What matters is the physical content that different valid descriptions predict and, where appropriate, the quantities that are invariant.
Here is the plain-English version. Say the same true sentence in English and in German. The words are completely different. The grammar is completely different.

What the sentence means has not changed at all. In physics, an observable is a quantity associated with a possible measurement. You have already watched this happen twice, in plainer clothes. In Chapter 2, two observers disagreed about distances, durations, even which of two events happened first — yet agreed on one
particular combination of those numbers, the invariant interval. Different measuring sticks. Same underlying fact.

In Chapter 11, we meet a particularly striking example from theoretical physics: in the AdS/CFT correspondence, a gravitational theory in a higher-dimensional spacetime can be mathematically equivalent to a quantum field theory without gravity on a lower-dimensional boundary. Two descriptions that look almost nothing alike, yet encode the same physics. It is a bit like Weinstein filing his patent notes in German and Trevor filing the same conclusions in English. Argue about the language all you like — the invention still works.
Penny’s contribution, from row F, is to notice the pattern and ask the next obvious question. If measuring sticks and entire mathematical languages are optional, what about a person’s own life story?
A “worldline” is the technical term for an object’s path through spacetime — in the human case, its physical history.

If that history is only one way of describing some deeper underlying state, then the story you tell about yourself may be exactly as optional as which ruler you used. Convenient. Not fundamental. This is why she texts Derek to stop investigating the clocks and start investigating the descriptions.

Without quite meaning to, she has beaten Sherlock the dolphin to the punch. His idea, delivered properly in Chapter 15, is that spacetime itself — and maybe even the order events happen in — might emerge from relationships, rather than being the stage those relationships happen on. And here is why this chapter earns its place directly before the tensors. A tensor exists purely to solve the problem Penny has just described: a mathematical object whose components are allowed to look totally different depending on your point of view, as long as the underlying thing they describe never changes.

As Chapter 15 puts it, a tensor is what happens when a vector gets promoted and starts having opinions about several directions at once. Which is, roughly, what just happened to Penny. What the reader should take away:

1. A film multiverse is a metaphor, nothing more — do not cite Marvel in an exam. 2. The idea actually worth keeping: rulers, languages, coordinate systems, and maybe even life stories, can all be different descriptions of one and the same underlying reality.
3. An “observable” is a quantity associated with a possible measurement — different valid descriptions must agree on the physical prediction.

4. This is exactly why, three chapters from now, General Relativity needs tensors: they are built specifically to say the same thing in every language. Jamie Lee Curtis, in accordance with the previously established Law of Conservation of Actresses, once again survives. Americans.
Keep this: The film is a metaphor for thinking about different descriptions, not an interpretation of quantum mechanics and not evidence for a multiverse.
Common trap: An analogy can illuminate a concept without proving the concept.
Quick test: Does a film about parallel universes establish a physical multiverse? No.
Chapter 13 — Curved Corridors and Tidal Gravity
The narrow corridor with twelve or thirteen doors is absurd. The underlying idea is not. In curved spacetime, local measurements can differ from measurements made over larger regions.

The crucial concept is tidal gravity. If gravity were perfectly uniform everywhere, you could locally reproduce its effects simply by accelerating your reference frame. But real gravitational fields vary from place to place.

That variation produces tidal effects. For example, Earth’s gravitational field is slightly stronger closer to Earth’s centre than farther away. Two freely falling objects initially moving together can therefore gradually move apart or together.

Mathematically, this is described by geodesic deviation. The narrow corridor joke is really about something quite respectable: Curvature reveals itself through how neighbouring free-fall paths behave relative to one another.
The narrow corridor did not actually gain a door. Probably.
Keep this: Curvature reveals itself through the relative behaviour of neighbouring free-fall paths; this is the physics of tidal gravity.
Common trap: ‘Gravity can be transformed away’ is only a local statement.
Quick test: What survives as evidence of curvature when a uniform gravitational field can be mimicked by acceleration? Tidal effects.
Chapter 14 — The Distant Train That Arrived Before It Left
That sounds like a violation of causality.
But before screaming “time machine”, we need to distinguish coordinate descriptions from actual causal structure.

In relativity, different observers can disagree about the temporal ordering of spacelike-separated events. For causally connected events, all inertial observers agree on their temporal order. Relativity does not let an ordinary cause arrive after its effect merely by changing coordinates. The light cone is the key.
For an event, spacetime can be divided into: its causal past, its causal future,

and regions that cannot be causally connected to it without exceeding the speed of light. The light-cone structure — what can causally influence what — is invariant. If Derek sees something that appears to happen before its cause, we should first ask:

Are those events actually causally connected? If not, the apparent reversal may simply be a consequence of the coordinate system. If they are causally connected and the story really reverses their order, then we have left ordinary Special Relativity and need some additional physics — or a very good explanation from the Relativistic Investigation Bureau.
At which point Derek should probably stop buying train tickets.

Keep this: Only spacelike-separated events can have their time ordering reversed between inertial frames without contradicting relativity. Common trap: Relativity does not allow the departure and arrival of one ordinary causal journey to swap order merely by changing coordinates. Quick test: If two events are causally connected, can an inertial observer simply transform them into the opposite temporal order? No.
Chapter 15 — The Dolphin and the Final Geometry
And now Sherlock. A dolphin communicating General Relativity telepathically is not established physics. The Einstein field equations are.
The central equation is: Gμν + Λgμν = 8πG/c⁴ Tμν. But before we explain that equation, we need to meet the things lurking inside it.
Tensors — Vectors’ Slightly More Ambitious Cousins A vector is already rather clever. It can tell you something like:
“Go three metres east and two metres north.”

It has components, and those components change when you change coordinates, but the underlying vector itself is the same physical thing. A tensor takes this idea one step further. At an introductory level, you can think of a tensor as a mathematical object that describes relationships between several directions at once.
Very roughly: Scalar: one number. Vector: a quantity with directional components.

Tensor: a quantity whose components describe relationships between directions. So, in the spirit of the Relativistic Investigation Bureau: A tensor is what happens when a vector gets promoted and starts having opinions about several directions simultaneously.
That is a useful analogy. It is not the formal mathematical definition.

A tensor is not simply a “higher-dimensional vector.” What matters is that its components obey specific transformation rules when we change coordinates, so that the underlying physical object remains well-defined.
And that is exactly why tensors are so useful in General Relativity. Spacetime can be curved. Coordinates can be awkward.

Observers can accelerate. Someone can be falling into a black hole while someone else is sitting safely in an office complaining about the coffee. We need mathematical objects that behave properly when we change coordinates.
Tensors do precisely that. The Metric Tensor The most important tensor to meet first is the metric tensor, written:
gμν. It tells us how spacetime is measured. In flat spacetime, the interval can be written, depending on sign convention, as:
ds² = −c²dt² + dx² + dy² + dz². In General Relativity, the metric can vary from place to place: ds² = gμν dxμ dxν.
Don’t let the Greek letters intimidate you. They are essentially telling us:
“Combine the changes in all the relevant directions according to the metric, and you get the spacetime interval.”
The metric is therefore rather like the instruction manual for measuring spacetime. It tells us about: distances,
and the geometry of spacetime itself. Once you know the metric, an enormous amount of physics follows. The Stress-Energy Tensor
Next comes: Tμν. This is the stress-energy tensor.
It describes the distribution and flow of physical quantities such as: energy density, momentum density,
pressure, stresses, and energy and momentum flowing through spacetime.
You can think of it as an extraordinarily sophisticated inventory of what matter and energy are doing.
Trevor once called it “the universe’s spreadsheet.”
Weinstein did not approve. He did, however, admit that the analogy wasn’t completely useless. The Curvature Tensors

Then things become progressively more tensorish. The Riemann curvature tensor contains the full local information about spacetime curvature. The Ricci tensor packages an important part of that curvature.

And the Einstein tensor, (Gμν), packages the relevant curvature information in precisely the form required by Einstein’s field equation. There is a reason physicists need all these objects. Curvature is not adequately described by saying:
“Space is a bit bent over there.”
That would be charming but mathematically inadequate. Curvature has structure. It can differ in different directions.

It can affect neighbouring paths differently. It can produce tidal effects. Tensors are the machinery that lets us describe all of this without losing the physics every time somebody changes coordinates.
And now, finally, we can look at the equation. Gμν + Λgμν = 8πG/c⁴ Tμν. The left-hand side is geometry.
The right-hand side is matter and energy.
The Einstein field equation therefore answered, in gloriously compressed mathematical form:
The geometry of spacetime is related to the distribution of matter and energy. Or, as Derek would put it:
“Matter tells spacetime how to curve, and spacetime tells matter how to behave.”
And for once, he would be right.
Nobody spoke for a moment. Even Trevor seemed to sense that the equation deserved it.
But Is General Relativity the Final Answer? Not necessarily.

General Relativity works extraordinarily well. But it does not appear to provide the complete description of nature at the quantum level. Black-hole singularities and the earliest moments of the universe are obvious warning signs.
This is where quantum gravity enters. Research programmes involving: quantum mechanics,
and emergent spacetime raise the possibility that spacetime itself might not be fundamental. That is an active research idea, not an established conclusion.
If a deeper theory eventually explains this, General Relativity would not become “wrong.”
It would become something like thermodynamics. Temperature is real. Pressure is real.
Neither is a fundamental microscopic object. They emerge from deeper physics. Spacetime might conceivably be similar.
And this brings us back to Weinstein’s original problem. Perhaps the final theory does not replace General Relativity. Perhaps it would explain why General Relativity works so remarkably well.
That would be a considerably more interesting achievement. And Sherlock, being a dolphin, naturally has no tenure problems.

Keep this: Tensors let physical laws be expressed in a coordinate-independent way; the Einstein field equation relates spacetime geometry to stress-energy. Common trap: Emergent spacetime and quantum gravity are active research areas, not completed theories. Quick test: What is on the geometric side of Einstein’s field equation? Curvature, packaged in the Einstein tensor plus the cosmological-constant term.
Let’s find out. If you can now explain why: 1. Two observers can disagree about elapsed time without either clock being broken,
2. The speed of light is the same for all inertial observers, 3. Special Relativity works locally inside General Relativity, 4. Gravity can be understood as spacetime geometry,
6. A singularity represents a breakdown of the classical description rather than merely “very strong gravity”,

7. Coordinate descriptions can disagree while invariant physics remains the same, 8. Holographic duality does not mean that the universe is literally a cinema screen, 9. Tensors are the mathematical language that lets us describe geometry and physical quantities consistently under coordinate changes,
and 10. An ordinary cucumber does not, in fact, constitute experimental evidence for quantum gravity— then congratulations.

You understand the essential ideas. You may now safely discuss relativity at dinner. You will, however, immediately discover that somebody knows a YouTube video proving Einstein was wrong. This is also part of the educational process.

Or you can have another piece of cake. The second option is generally shorter, and in Derek’s experience no less illuminating. The universe, for its part, remains indifferent to both choices. And there is one final question.

Derek’s question. The question that has been lurking underneath the entire book: If space and time can be observer-dependent, if gravity is geometry, if geometry might itself emerge from deeper physics, and if different descriptions can encode the same reality…
what, exactly, is reality? Well. That’s the problem.
We haven’t finished. But the good news is that neither has the universe. Which is rather reassuring.
